v0.8.0 made fufu work for a fleet of worktrees. What it did not do is get fufu invoked. fufu captures only when something calls it, and everything that calls it — an agent client's tool hook, a shell prompt, the repository's own pre-commit runner — sits outside fufu and has to be met on its own terms. This release is that boundary.

**One grammar for wiring, one for events**

`ff hook <agent|shell|editor> <install|uninstall|list|trigger> [name]` was a nested grammar over a flat set of facts. It collapses into two verbs a person types and one a client calls. `ff hook` and `ff unhook` take flat slugs — claude, codex, cursor, gemini, bash, zsh, fish — and `ff trigger <source>` is the machine surface. Bare `ff hook` reports what is on this machine and asks; `--all` skips the question, `-l` reports and stops.

The two namespaces differ on purpose. `hook` names a thing you integrate with; `trigger` names an event source, which is finer-grained — all three shell slugs install rc lines calling one `ff trigger shell`, and a client whose payload cannot identify its own event is `<vendor>-<event>`, split on the first `-`. The contracts differ to match: an unknown slug is a real error and a wiring failure is loud, while an unknown source exits 0 in silence, which is what makes a fufu trigger safe to wire into a client fufu has never heard of.

Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI join Claude Code. `crates/ff-cli/src/integ/` is one client-neutral core — a neutral event, one capture pipeline, one briefing text — behind four thin protocol adapters that translate a payload in and wrap the briefing on the way out. What gets written is per-adapter rather than a user choice: Claude Code takes a plugin directory fufu owns outright, the other clients take entries merged into their own settings file, and the shells take marked lines in an rc file. A line somebody wrote by hand is detected, reported, and never touched — `ff hook` leaves it, `ff unhook` leaves it.

`ff doctor` folds every wiring row out of the same `integ::statuses()` vector `ff hook -l` renders, so the two commands cannot disagree about what is wired — which is exactly what the two hand-written enumerations used to allow. `--fix` gains one case: a wiring that still captures but is written in a spelling fufu no longer writes gets rewritten, because a stored string is otherwise only refreshed when somebody happens to run the installer again.

Bare `ff trigger` brings back the manual snapshot verb that retired when bare `ff` became the map: capture and stop, with `-m` to say what it is for.

**A manual an agent can reach**

The once-per-session briefing is the only spelling lesson an agent gets, and it is capped by test because every session pays for it whether or not it needs it. That cap left everything past "commit, undo, don't write with git" nowhere to live: an agent needing `ff resolve`, `ff edit`, `ff lift`, or the difference between `ff undo` and `ff op revert` had no route to them, so it reached for `ff git rebase -i` and fought the model.

The two texts now split by what they cost. The briefing keeps the always-on contract and nothing else — four writing verbs, the git rule, the three readers, and a pointer at `--help` — and comes down from 1,156 bytes to 667, with the budget lowered to 800 so the reduction is a contract rather than slack. Everything else moves to a skill fufu ships: the model, a recovery decision table, rewriting, held rewrites, parking, remotes, the landmines, the machine surface. It costs nothing until a client decides the situation calls for it, and it names each verb's own `--help` as the authority rather than restating one.

Delivery is the directory story fufu's Claude Code adapter already tells. Claude Code's skill rides inside the plugin fufu owns outright, at `skills/fufu/SKILL.md`, so install and uninstall stay write-whole and remove-whole. Codex takes a directory of its own under `~/.codex/skills/`, independent of the settings file it does not own. Cursor and Gemini read no skills directory and are not told to read one: the briefing's pointer at the skill is asked of the adapter at print time, because an install and a disk can disagree, and naming a manual that is not there is worse than saying nothing.

For everywhere else there is `ff hook --skill`, which prints the skill verbatim to stdout and stops, so `ff hook --skill > ~/.cursor/rules/fufu.md` produces a file byte-identical to the one an install writes. The hole it fills is wider than those two clients: `ff trigger <unknown>` exits 0 in silence precisely so a fufu trigger is safe to wire into a client fufu has never heard of, and the extension point was inviting third parties and then offering them capture with no way to get the manual. `ff --help` now closes with a block telling an agent to run it, guarded with "SKIP if fufu's skill is already in your context" — one route, not three, and what makes an agent that was never briefed find the manual at all.

Both texts are prose an agent reads as instructions, and both rot the silent way when the surface moves, so both are guarded: a test extracts every command either one spells and parses it with clap, failing on a flag that no longer exists or a verb that has gone hidden. It caught two while this was being written.

**Your hooks see the index populated**

Every hook-runner keyed on staging — lefthook, lint-staged, husky, the pre-commit framework — silently did nothing under `ff commit`. fufu keeps `.git/index` written to a tree, so during an open change it describes what the *last* commit took and `git diff --cached` is empty; lefthook's `{staged_files}` resolves to an empty list, every job is skipped, the runner exits 0, and the commit lands with nothing having run. Telling users to rewrite a config that is intentional and shared with git users would be fufu exporting its problem.

Git already does what is needed here: `commit -a` and `commit -- <path>` both populate the index before running `pre-commit`, and roll it back when the hook declines. So a close writes the index to the tree it is about to commit just before the first hook, and restores it byte-for-byte when the close does not land. The index stays a derived compatibility surface the user never sees or maintains — it was only being written at the wrong moment.

The restore is byte-exact rather than a rewrite to HEAD's tree, because a user may have their own `git add` state, which fufu tolerates, and a refused close must not destroy it. A partial `ff commit <paths>` stages exactly what is landing, as git's pathspec form does. A repository with no hooks pays two `stat` calls.

One divergence from git stands, in fufu's favor and left alone: a formatter's fixes land via the worktree re-scan rather than via anything the hook staged, so lefthook's `stage_fixed: true` is decorative here, where under git a formatter that rewrites without re-staging loses its fixes.

**`ff collide` answers one pair**

The verb shipped in v0.8.0 carrying two products and neither had an audience. The all-pairs matrix over every local branch was unreadable past a couple of dozen names, and the greedy clear set folded out of it existed to feed a scheduler fufu does not have. The sideways pitch — two people seeing each other before either has committed — was never available: open changes are read from `refs/fufu/snap/<branch>`, a local ref namespace, so it reaches across worktrees on one machine and never across people.

`ff collide <other>` now compares the branch you are on against that one, and `ff collide <a> <b>` names both sides. The judging is unchanged: all merge bases rather than the best one, and the merge inside an object-memory clone. What went is the matrix and the ranking that fed it. `--all` and `-n` are gone, one name or two is enforced by clap, and a branch named against itself is refused with `usage/collide-same-branch` rather than answered clear. Collide also gains the long help page it was the only reader verb to lack.

Both performance cliffs went with it. The matrix ran n(n-1)/2 merges sequentially, each costing time proportional to the whole tree rather than the diff — 200 branches over a 5,000-file tree took two minutes. The clear set was worse in shape, rescanning every pair once per admitted name, so a mostly-clear repository paid O(n^4) string comparisons and 400 clear branches took 41.6s against 10.1s for 400 colliding ones where the check short-circuits. Two names is 5ms and 61ms on those same fixtures.

The set-building this leaves behind belongs to tower, which has the queue, the flying set, and `ff watch --all` to invalidate on. A verdict is a fact about two trees; a set is a fact about a queue. Only the first is fufu's to answer.

**Smaller things**

The ambient status-line channel is gone. `fufu.ambient` leaves the config registry and the code that rendered on it leaves the shell adapter. The prompt hook itself stays exactly where it was and is now pure capture — which is what the zero-spawn budget on `ff trigger shell` always said it was.

Two clippy lints that arrived with Rust 1.98 are fixed. rust-toolchain.toml tracks stable, so a new stable is a new lint set, and `-D warnings` turns that into a red main the day the runner image moves.

**Numbers**

9 commits over v0.8.0, +6,392/−2,622 across 46 files. 1,430 workspace tests, up from 1,364. 110 `ff explain` ids, up from 108.
